First Kings opens in a bedroom in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. King ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, the warrior who united the tribes and took the city for his capital, is now old and cannot keep warm. Outside the palace, one of his sons is already holding a feast to celebrate his own accession. The question that hung over the last years of Second ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧, who will sit on David's throne after him, is about to be answered.

The book follows directly from ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧, and in the Hebrew Bible First and Second Kings were a single work, divided later into two scrolls. Together they cover about four hundred years, from ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s death a little before nine hundred and seventy years before Christ to the fall of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. The book does not name its author, and Jewish tradition gives it to the prophet ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧. The account was completed during the exile, since its last scene takes place in Babylon, and its writer was looking back over the whole history of the kings. The writer drew on older records and names them from time to time, the book of the acts of ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ and the chronicles of the kings of Israel and of Judah, sending readers there for details he chose to leave out.

That choice matters. Kings is not a complete political history. Some reigns that were important to the wider world are passed over in a few sentences, while others are told at length because of what they reveal about Israel's faithfulness to God. Each king is measured by a single question: did he do what was right in the eyes of the Lord, like his father ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, or did he lead the people into the worship of other gods? Running through the book is the voice of the prophets, men who stand before kings with the word of the Lord, and whose predictions are later noted as fulfilled.

The first eleven chapters belong to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧, ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s son by ⟦p:bathsheba_416|Bathsheba⟧. He comes to the throne through a palace struggle, secures it with hard measures, and then asks God for wisdom to govern. The kingdom he inherits from David stretches from the ⟦l:euphrates_421|Euphrates⟧ to the border of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, and under Solomon it enjoys peace, trade and fame. His greatest work is the temple in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, built with cedar from ⟦l:lebanon_720|Lebanon⟧ and gold from distant lands, the house for the Lord's name that David was not permitted to build. The books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs are linked with his name. But the same chapters also record the heavy labour that built his projects, his many foreign wives, and the turning of his heart in old age to their gods.

After ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s death, in chapter twelve, the kingdom breaks in two. The ten northern tribes reject his son ⟦p:rehoboam_2412|Rehoboam⟧ and follow ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧, a former official of Solomon's, and they keep the name Israel. Rehoboam is left with Judah and the small tribe of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧, ruling from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. From here the listener needs to keep two kingdoms in mind. In the south, Judah keeps the line of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, one dynasty from start to finish. In the north, Israel has no fixed royal house; its throne passes by assassination and coup from one family to another, and its capital moves from Shechem to ⟦l:tirzah_1170|Tirzah⟧ and finally to ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧ and ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧, so that his people need not go to Jerusalem to worship, and the writer judges every northern king after him by whether he turned from the sins of Jeroboam.

The writer moves back and forth between the two kingdoms, dating each king's accession by the year of the king reigning in the other. It can feel like a tangle of names, but the pattern is steady: an opening note on when a king began to reign and how long, a verdict on his faithfulness, the events chosen for telling, and a closing note on his death and burial.

The last part of the book slows down dramatically. In the north, Omri founds a powerful dynasty and builds ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, and his son ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ marries ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧, a princess of ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧, who brings with her the worship of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧. Against them stands the prophet ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧, a rough figure from ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧ east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, who appears without introduction and declares a drought. The contest between Elijah and the house of Ahab, on ⟦l:mount_carmel_831|Mount Carmel⟧ and beyond, fills most of the closing chapters. The book ends with Ahab's death in battle against the Arameans and the reigns of the next kings in both kingdoms. Elijah's story, and the long decline of both kingdoms, will continue in Second Kings.
1:
⟦p:david_994|David⟧ is old and failing, and his servants bring a young woman from ⟦l:shunem_1089|Shunem⟧, in the north, named ⟦p:abishag_49|Abishag⟧, to care for him. The king's weakness leaves the question of succession wide open, for David has named no heir before the people.

⟦p:amnon_232|Amnon⟧ and ⟦p:absalom_59|Absalom⟧ are dead, and next in age comes ⟦p:adonijah_97|Adonijah⟧, the son of ⟦p:haggith_1353|Haggith⟧. Like Absalom before him, he is handsome and ambitious, and he too acquires chariots, horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him. The narrator adds that ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ never once corrected him. Adonijah has gathered powerful allies: ⟦p:joab_1617|Joab⟧, the long-serving commander of the army, and ⟦p:abiathar_20|Abiathar⟧ the priest, who has been with David since his fugitive days. Others stand apart, among them ⟦p:zadok_2973|Zadok⟧ the priest, ⟦p:benaiah_439|Benaiah⟧ the commander of the royal guard, and ⟦p:nathan_2153|Nathan⟧ the prophet.

When ⟦p:adonijah_97|Adonijah⟧ holds a great sacrificial feast at ⟦l:en-rogel_395|En-rogel⟧, a spring just below ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and leaves out these men and his brother ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧, ⟦p:nathan_2153|Nathan⟧ sees the danger at once. He goes to ⟦p:bathsheba_416|Bathsheba⟧, Solomon's mother, with a plan. Within a single day, the city will hear two different celebrations.
2:
⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ has been anointed at the Gihon spring and seated on his father's throne, and ⟦p:adonijah_97|Adonijah⟧, who clung to the horns of the altar for safety, has been sent home. Now ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s life is ending. Like ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ before him, he gives a final charge to his successor.

The first part of that charge looks back to the Law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and to the promise God made to ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s house. The second part is more personal and harder to hear. David reminds ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ of unfinished business from the years of Second ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧: ⟦p:joab_1617|Joab⟧ and the two commanders he murdered, ⟦p:abner_57|Abner⟧ and ⟦p:amasa_207|Amasa⟧; ⟦p:barzillai_411|Barzillai⟧ of ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, who fed the king in exile; and ⟦p:shimei_2684|Shimei⟧, the Benjamite who cursed him on the road out of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.

⟦p:david_994|David⟧ dies and is buried in the ⟦l:jerusalem_636|City of David⟧ after reigning forty years. The rest of the chapter shows the new king making his position secure. One by one, ⟦p:adonijah_97|Adonijah⟧, ⟦p:abiathar_20|Abiathar⟧, ⟦p:joab_1617|Joab⟧ and ⟦p:shimei_2684|Shimei⟧ come before him, and ⟦p:benaiah_439|Benaiah⟧, captain of the guard, is kept busy. Abiathar is sent away to his estate at ⟦l:anathoth_63|Anathoth⟧, a village just north of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ that will later be the home of the prophet ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, and the writer sees in his removal the fulfilment of the word spoken long ago against the house of ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧. By the chapter's close, the kingdom is firmly in ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s hand.
3:
⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s throne is secure, and now we see what kind of king he will be. The chapter begins with two notes that are easy to pass over. He makes a marriage alliance with ⟦p:pharaoh_2332|Pharaoh⟧, king of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, a sign of how far Israel's standing has risen. And the people, along with Solomon himself, are still offering sacrifices at the high places, local hilltop shrines, because there is not yet a temple. The writer marks this as a shortcoming, and the high places will be measured against king after king in the chapters to come.

The greatest of these shrines is at ⟦l:gibeon_470|Gibeon⟧, a few miles north-west of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, where, as Chronicles tells us, the old tabernacle of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧' day then stood. There ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ offers a thousand burnt offerings, and that night the Lord appears to him in a dream with an open invitation: ask for whatever you want. Solomon's answer, and God's response to it, set the tone for the opening years of his reign.

The chapter ends with a case brought before the new king by two women who live in the same house. It has become the most famous judgement in the Bible, and it shows all Israel that the wisdom ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ asked for has been given.
4:
After the dream at ⟦l:gibeon_470|Gibeon⟧ and the case of the two mothers, the writer steps back to show the shape of ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s government. This chapter reads like an administrative record, and in a sense it is one, but it also paints a picture of a kingdom at the height of its prosperity.

First comes the list of his chief officials. Some names carry over from ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s court: ⟦p:benaiah_439|Benaiah⟧, now in command of the army, and ⟦p:zadok_2973|Zadok⟧ the priest, whose son ⟦p:azariah_373|Azariah⟧ appears here as priest too. Two sons of a man named ⟦p:nathan_2153|Nathan⟧ hold high office, one of them as priest and adviser to the king. Then come twelve district governors, each responsible for supplying the royal household for one month of the year. Their districts do not simply follow the old tribal boundaries, and Judah has a governor of its own.

The second half of the chapter widens the view: a kingdom reaching from the ⟦l:euphrates_421|Euphrates⟧ to the border of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, a people eating and drinking and rejoicing, every man under his own vine and fig tree. It ends with ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s wisdom and fame, his three thousand proverbs and more than a thousand songs, and visitors coming from every nation to hear him.
5:
⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s kingdom is at peace, and he turns to the great work his father longed to do. In chapter seven of Second ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧, the Lord told ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ that his son would build a house for his name. Now that son is on the throne.

The help he needs comes from the north. ⟦p:hiram_1532|Hiram⟧, king of ⟦l:tyre_1184|Tyre⟧, the wealthy Phoenician port on the Mediterranean coast, had been a friend of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ and supplied cedar for his palace. The mountains of ⟦l:lebanon_720|Lebanon⟧ behind Tyre and ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧ were famous across the ancient world for their great cedars, and the Phoenicians were the finest timber workers and seafarers of the age. ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ proposes an arrangement, and Hiram responds warmly. The logs will be floated down the coast in rafts, and Solomon will pay in wheat and olive oil.

The rest of the chapter describes the workforce. ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ conscripts tens of thousands of Israelites to work in ⟦l:lebanon_720|Lebanon⟧ in monthly shifts, and many more to carry loads and quarry stone in the hills. The man in charge of this forced labour is ⟦p:adoniram_102|Adoniram⟧, and the resentment it stirred will one day help tear the kingdom apart.
6:
The timber is coming down the coast from ⟦l:lebanon_720|Lebanon⟧ and the great stones are being cut in the quarries. Now the building begins. The writer marks the date with unusual care: the fourth year of ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s reign, the four hundred and eightieth year after Israel came out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. The temple is presented as the long-awaited end of the road that began at the exodus.

The measurements are given in cubits, a cubit being roughly the length of a forearm. The temple itself was not enormous, about twenty-seven metres long and nine wide, because worshippers gathered in the courtyards outside. Its plan follows the pattern of the tabernacle in the wilderness, on a larger scale: a porch at the front, a main hall, and at the back a perfect cube, the ⟦l:most_holy_place_827|inner sanctuary⟧ or ⟦l:most_holy_place_827|Most Holy Place⟧, where the ark of the covenant would rest beneath two great cherubim of gold-covered olive wood.

Inside, cedar panelling carved with gourds and flowers is overlaid with gold, so that not a single stone can be seen. In the middle of the building account comes a word from the Lord to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧, a reminder that what matters most is not the house but the obedience of the king who builds it. The work takes seven years.
7:
The temple is finished, but before the writer describes its furnishings he turns to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s other building projects in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. The contrast is quietly made: the temple took seven years, and the king's own palace took thirteen.

The palace complex had several parts. The largest was the ⟦l:lebanon_585|House of the Forest of Lebanon⟧, so named for its rows of cedar pillars, which served as a great hall and, as we later learn, an armoury. There was a colonnade, a Hall of Justice where ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ sat to judge, his own residence, and a separate palace for his Egyptian queen.

Then the account returns to the temple and to a master craftsman in bronze named ⟦p:hiram_1533|Huram⟧, not ⟦p:hiram_1533|Hiram⟧ the king of ⟦l:tyre_1184|Tyre⟧ but a man of mixed descent, the son of a widow from the tribe of ⟦p:naphtali_2149|Naphtali⟧ and a father from Tyre. His work is described piece by piece: two great bronze pillars at the entrance, given the names Jachin and ⟦p:boaz_519|Boaz⟧; an enormous bronze basin called the Sea, resting on twelve bronze oxen; and ten wheeled stands with basins. These bronze works will appear once more in the story, at the very end of Second Kings, and the listener may wish to remember them.
8:
The temple and all its furnishings are complete. Now ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ gathers the elders of every tribe and family to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ for its dedication. It is the seventh month, the season of the autumn Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel remembered its years of living in tents in the wilderness.

The first task is to bring the ark of the covenant up from the ⟦l:jerusalem_636|City of David⟧, the lower part of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ where ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ had placed it in a tent, to its new home on the higher ground to the north. The writer notes that the ark contains only the two stone tablets ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ placed in it at ⟦l:horeb_576|Horeb⟧, the mountain also known as ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧. When the ark is set in its place, something happens that recalls the day the tabernacle was completed in the wilderness, and the priests cannot continue their work.

Most of the chapter is given to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s words: a blessing on the people, and then one of the longest prayers in the Bible, spoken with his hands spread out toward heaven. Solomon asks the Lord to hear whatever prayers are made toward this house, in war, drought, famine and plague, even from foreigners and even from captives in a distant land. Those who first read the finished book of Kings were themselves exiles, and they would have heard that last request with particular force.
9:
The temple and the palace are complete, after twenty years of building, and ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ has done everything he set out to do. At this high point, the Lord appears to him a second time, as he did at ⟦l:gibeon_470|Gibeon⟧ at the beginning of his reign.

The message answers ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s prayer. God has consecrated the house and will put his name there. But the promise comes with a solemn condition, addressed to Solomon and to his sons after him, and its warning is spelled out in vivid detail. The rest of the book of Kings will show how that warning came true.

The remainder of the chapter gathers notes on the wider reign. ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ settles accounts with ⟦p:hiram_1532|Hiram⟧ of ⟦l:tyre_1184|Tyre⟧ by giving him twenty towns in ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, which do not please him. There is a record of the forced labour that built Solomon's projects, including the fortified cities of ⟦l:hazor_545|Hazor⟧, ⟦l:megiddo_777|Megiddo⟧ and ⟦l:gezer_463|Gezer⟧, guarding the great roads through the land. Gezer, we learn, came to Solomon as a dowry when ⟦p:pharaoh_2332|Pharaoh⟧ captured it and gave it to his daughter. And Solomon builds a fleet at ⟦l:ezion-geber_423|Ezion-geber⟧, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, which sails with Phoenician crews to a distant land of gold called ⟦l:ophir_911|Ophir⟧.
10:
⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s fame is spreading far beyond Israel, and this chapter shows it at its height. It opens with a royal visitor: the queen of ⟦l:sheba_1067|Sheba⟧. Her kingdom lay in south-western ⟦l:arabia_80|Arabia⟧, in what is now Yemen, a land grown rich on the trade in frankincense, myrrh and spices that travelled north by camel caravan. She has come a very long way.

She comes, the writer says, to test ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ with hard questions, and she brings a great caravan of gifts. What she sees in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ leaves her breathless. Her words in praise of Solomon's God are among the warmest spoken by any foreigner in the Old Testament, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ would later recall her journey in his own preaching.

After her departure the chapter turns to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s wealth: shields of beaten gold, an ivory throne with lions on its steps, ships that bring back gold, silver, ivory and apes, and horses and chariots traded from ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ and from Kue, in what is now southern Turkey. The listener who knows the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ may remember that it warned Israel's kings against gathering many horses from Egypt, many wives and great amounts of silver and gold. Two of those three are described here. The third comes next.
11:
The splendour of chapter ten is still fresh when this chapter opens with a single word that changes its direction: however. ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ loved many foreign women. ⟦p:pharaoh_2332|Pharaoh⟧'s daughter has been mentioned before; now we hear of wives from ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammon⟧, ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧, ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧ and the Hittites, seven hundred wives of royal birth in all. The law had warned that such marriages would turn Israel's heart to other gods, and in Solomon's old age that is exactly what happens. On a hill east of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, within sight of the city, he builds shrines for the gods of his wives.

The Lord's word to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ follows, announcing that the kingdom will be torn away, though not in his own lifetime, and not entirely. Then the writer introduces three adversaries. Two come from beyond Israel's borders: ⟦p:hadad_1339|Hadad⟧, a prince of ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧ who had grown up in exile in ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, and ⟦p:rezon_2437|Rezon⟧, who seized power in ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧. The third comes from within.

He is ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧ son of ⟦p:nebat_2165|Nebat⟧, a capable young man of the tribe of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, whom ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ put in charge of the whole labour force of the house of ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧, his own people. On the road outside ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ he meets a prophet, ⟦p:ahijah_135|Ahijah⟧ of ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧, who is wearing a new cloak. What Ahijah does with it, and what he says, will shape the history of the next two centuries.
12:
⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ is dead after forty years on the throne. In ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧ his son ⟦p:rehoboam_2412|Rehoboam⟧'s succession is not in doubt, but the northern tribes have yet to accept him. So Rehoboam goes north to ⟦l:shechem_1069|Shechem⟧, the ancient town in the hills of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ where ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ once gathered the tribes to renew their covenant with the Lord. The people's representatives meet him there, and with them comes ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧, back from his refuge in ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧.

They bring one request: lighten the heavy yoke your father laid on us. ⟦p:rehoboam_2412|Rehoboam⟧ takes three days and consults two groups of advisers, the old men who served ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ and the young men he grew up with. His answer divides the nation. Listeners who remember Sheba's rebellion in Second ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ will recognise the cry that goes up in reply.

From this point on there are two kingdoms. In the north, the ten tribes keep the name Israel and make ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧ their king. In the south, ⟦p:rehoboam_2412|Rehoboam⟧ rules ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧, with ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧, from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. Jeroboam now faces a problem: the temple, and the great feasts, are in his rival's capital. His solution, set up at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧ in the south of his kingdom and at ⟦l:dan_323|Dan⟧ in the far north, will be called the sin of Jeroboam for the rest of the book, and his words to the people echo those once spoken over ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s golden calf at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧.
13:
⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧ is standing beside his new altar at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, about to burn incense at the feast he has devised. Bethel was an ancient holy place, the spot where ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧ once dreamed of a stairway to heaven, and it lay only a few miles north of the border with ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧.

Into this scene comes a man of God from ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧, sent by the word of the Lord, and he speaks not to the king but to the altar. His message names a king of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s line who will one day come to this place. The name is ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧, and the listener will meet him three hundred years later, near the end of Second Kings. The prophecy is confirmed at once by a sign, and ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧ himself is caught up in it.

The man of God has been given strict instructions about his journey home, and the rest of the chapter is one of the strangest stories in Kings. It involves an old prophet who lives in ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, a meal, a lie, and a lion on the road. It is a sobering account of what it means to carry the word of the Lord, and of how seriously that word is to be taken. The chapter ends by returning to ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧, and to the verdict that will hang over his house.
14:
⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧ has been warned at his own altar, and he has not changed course. Now trouble comes to his own household. His son ⟦p:abijah_35|Abijah⟧ falls ill, and Jeroboam sends his wife, in disguise, to the prophet who first promised him the kingdom: ⟦p:ahijah_135|Ahijah⟧, the old man of ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧. Jeroboam's court is now at ⟦l:tirzah_1170|Tirzah⟧, a town in the hills north-east of Shechem, which will serve as the northern capital for the next few reigns.

⟦p:ahijah_135|Ahijah⟧'s eyes are dim with age and he cannot see, but the Lord has told him who is coming. His message reaches beyond the sick boy to the house of ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧, and to the whole northern kingdom, which will one day be scattered beyond the ⟦l:euphrates_421|Euphrates⟧. The exile of the north is foretold here, two centuries before it came.

The second half of the chapter crosses the border to Judah. Here we see for the first time the pattern the writer will use for the kings of Judah from now on: the king's age, the length of his reign, his mother's name, a verdict on his faithfulness, some selected events, and his burial. ⟦p:rehoboam_2412|Rehoboam⟧'s reign is summed up briefly, and it includes an invasion by ⟦p:shishak_2712|Shishak⟧, king of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, the pharaoh who once sheltered ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧, whose own inscription recording the campaign still survives.
15:
The story now moves briskly, crossing the border and back as one king follows another.

In Judah, ⟦p:rehoboam_2412|Rehoboam⟧ is followed by his son ⟦p:abijah_38|Abijam⟧, who reigns only three years. Then comes ⟦p:asa_318|Asa⟧, who reigns for forty-one, the first king of Judah to be praised for doing what was right in the eyes of the Lord, as ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ had done. He clears away idols and even removes his own grandmother from her position as queen mother. The high places, the writer notes, still remain.

In the north, ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧'s son ⟦p:nadab_2129|Nadab⟧ reigns for two years before he is assassinated by ⟦p:baasha_589|Baasha⟧, a man of the tribe of ⟦p:issachar_645|Issachar⟧, while the army is besieging the Philistine town of ⟦l:gibbethon_465|Gibbethon⟧. With this the pattern of the northern kingdom is set: one family seizes the throne from another, and ⟦p:ahijah_136|Ahijah⟧'s words against Jeroboam's house come true. Meanwhile Baasha and ⟦p:asa_318|Asa⟧ are at war. Baasha fortifies ⟦l:ramah_972|Ramah⟧, only a few miles north of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and Asa turns for help to ⟦p:ben-hadad_452|Ben-hadad⟧, king of ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧ in ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧. It is the first of many times that the Arameans of Damascus will be drawn into Israel's affairs.
16:
⟦p:baasha_589|Baasha⟧ now rules the northern kingdom from ⟦l:tirzah_1170|Tirzah⟧, but his house will not last much longer than ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧'s. This chapter moves quickly through a time of turmoil in the north, while in Judah King ⟦p:asa_318|Asa⟧'s long reign continues.

A prophet named ⟦p:jehu_816|Jehu⟧ son of ⟦p:hanani_1379|Hanani⟧ brings ⟦p:baasha_589|Baasha⟧ a message very like the one ⟦p:ahijah_135|Ahijah⟧ brought to ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧. Baasha's son ⟦p:elah_1045|Elah⟧ reigns for two years and is murdered while drunk by ⟦p:zimri_3088|Zimri⟧, one of his chariot commanders. Zimri's reign lasts only seven days. The army proclaims its own commander, ⟦p:omri_2243|Omri⟧, as king, and after a period of civil war against a rival named Tibni, Omri takes the throne.

⟦p:omri_2243|Omri⟧ receives only a few verses, but he was one of the most important kings of the north. He moves the capital to a new city on a hill he buys: ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, which will remain Israel's capital until the end of the kingdom. For generations afterwards, Assyrian records called Israel the house of Omri. Then the chapter introduces his son ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, and with him ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧, the daughter of the king of ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧, a devoted worshipper of the Phoenician storm god ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧. In Samaria Ahab builds a temple to Baal, and a few verses later a prophet walks into the story.
17:
⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ and ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧ have brought the worship of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ into the heart of Israel, with a temple in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ itself. Now, with no introduction beyond his name and his homeland, a prophet appears before the king. He is ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ the Tishbite, from ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, the rough hill country east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧. His name means my God is the Lord, and his first words are a challenge.

⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ was worshipped as the god of storm and rain, the one who made the land fertile. ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ announces that there will be neither dew nor rain except at his word. The contest between the Lord and Baal has begun, and it will be fought on Baal's own ground.

Then ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ disappears from ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧'s sight. The Lord sends him first to hide by a brook east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, and later, when it dries up, to a town called ⟦l:zarephath_1242|Zarephath⟧ on the coast near ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧. That is ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧'s homeland, the heart of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧'s territory, and there Elijah is taken in by a poor widow who is down to her last handful of flour. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ would later remind his hearers in ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧ that, of all the widows in Israel, Elijah was sent to this one. The chapter tells of her household, and of a crisis that tests her faith in the man of God under her roof.
18:
The drought has lasted into its third year, and the famine in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ is severe. The word of the Lord comes to ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ again: go and show yourself to ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, and I will send rain.

Before ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ meets the king, he meets ⟦p:obadiah_2215|Obadiah⟧, who manages ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧'s palace. He is not the prophet whose short book appears later in the Bible, but a court official who has quietly feared the Lord all his life and has risked his own safety to protect the Lord's prophets from ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧. Ahab and Obadiah are out searching the land for any grass to keep the royal horses alive, and Obadiah's fear when he sees Elijah shows how hard Ahab has been hunting him.

Then comes the most famous scene in ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧'s life. He calls for all Israel, and for the four hundred and fifty prophets of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧, to gather on ⟦l:mount_carmel_831|Mount Carmel⟧, a long ridge running down to the Mediterranean near what is now Haifa. ⟦l:carmel_278|Carmel⟧ lay on the border between Israel and ⟦l:phenicia_944|Phoenicia⟧, and on its heights there was once an altar of the Lord, now torn down. Elijah puts a simple question to the people about whom they will follow, and proposes a test. By evening, clouds are rising from the sea, and Elijah is running ahead of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧'s chariot to the royal city of ⟦l:jezreel_643|Jezreel⟧.
19:
After the fire on ⟦l:carmel_278|Carmel⟧ and the rain that ended the drought, it might seem that ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧'s worship in Israel is finished. It is not. ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ tells ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧ what ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ has done, and she sends him a message: by this time tomorrow, you will be dead.

⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ runs. He goes south out of Israel altogether, through Judah to ⟦l:beersheba_170|Beersheba⟧ on the edge of the desert, and then alone into the wilderness beyond. The man who stood against hundreds of prophets now lies down under a broom tree in the desert and asks to die. What follows is gentle and unexpected, and it leads him on a journey of forty days and nights to ⟦l:horeb_576|Horeb⟧, the ⟦l:horeb_576|mountain of God⟧, also called ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, where the Lord once spoke to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧. Like Moses before him, Elijah will stand on the mountain as the Lord passes by, though not in the way he might expect.

⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ is given a new task, to anoint three men: a king for ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧, a king for Israel, and a prophet to succeed him. Their names will matter in Second Kings. Elijah finds the third of them first, a farmer named ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧, ploughing behind twelve teams of oxen, and throws his cloak around him.
20:
⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ has gone to anoint his successor, and he steps out of the story for a while. The scene shifts to war. ⟦p:ben-hadad_452|Ben-hadad⟧, king of ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧ in ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, marches on Israel with a great army and thirty-two allied kings, local rulers under his authority, and lays siege to ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. Ben-hadad was a name borne by more than one king of Damascus, and it is a name the listener will hear again.

⟦p:ben-hadad_452|Ben-hadad⟧'s demands begin as harsh and become humiliating, and ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, backed by his elders, finally refuses. Then something unexpected happens. A prophet of the Lord, unnamed, comes to Ahab with a promise of victory. Despite everything Ahab has done, the Lord has not abandoned Israel, and he intends Ahab to know who he is.

There are two campaigns in this chapter, the first at ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ and the second a year later at ⟦l:aphek_73|Aphek⟧, where the Arameans choose to fight on the plain because they believe Israel's God rules only the hills. The decisive moment, though, comes after the second battle, when ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ must decide what to do with the defeated king of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧. Then another prophet waits by the road, disguised as a wounded soldier, with a story that, like ⟦p:nathan_2153|Nathan⟧'s to ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, leads the king to pass sentence on himself. Ahab goes home to Samaria sullen and angry.
21:
⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ has gone home sullen and angry after the prophet's rebuke, and the next chapter finds him in the same mood again, this time over something much smaller. Next to his palace in ⟦l:jezreel_643|Jezreel⟧, the royal city in the fertile valley north of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, lies a vineyard belonging to a man named ⟦p:naboth_2127|Naboth⟧. Ahab wants it for a vegetable garden, and he makes what seems a fair offer.

⟦p:naboth_2127|Naboth⟧'s refusal is not stubbornness. In Israel, family land was an inheritance from the Lord, divided among the tribes in ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧'s day and meant to stay within the family for ever. Naboth will not sell what belongs to his fathers. ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ accepts the answer, but sulks. ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧, the daughter of a king of ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧, does not accept it at all. Her husband reigns over Israel, she reminds him, and she knows how to use Israel's own institutions to get what she wants.

The chapter is short and terrible, and it brings ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ back into the story. He finds ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ in the vineyard itself. The words he speaks there will be remembered, and fulfilled, in the chapters and years to come. Then Ahab responds in a way that surprises even the reader, and the Lord's answer to that response is the chapter's final word.
22:
Three years of peace have passed between Israel and ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧, the treaty ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ made with Ben-hadad holding. The Bible does not mention it, but Assyrian records tell us that around this time Ahab and the king of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ fought side by side against the Assyrian king Shalmaneser at Qarqar in ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧. ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, the great power from the ⟦l:tigris_1163|Tigris⟧, will loom ever larger over the rest of Kings.

Now the old rivalry returns. The town of ⟦l:ramoth-gilead_984|Ramoth-gilead⟧, east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, is still in Aramean hands, and ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ wants it back. He has a new ally: ⟦p:jehoshaphat_808|Jehoshaphat⟧, the son of ⟦p:asa_318|Asa⟧, king of Judah. After decades of war between the two kingdoms, the royal houses of Israel and Judah are now at peace, and as Second Kings will show, they have been joined by marriage. Jehoshaphat is willing to fight, but he wants first to hear from the Lord.

Four hundred prophets assure the kings of victory. ⟦p:jehoshaphat_808|Jehoshaphat⟧ asks whether there is not another prophet, and ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ admits there is one, ⟦p:micaiah_2054|Micaiah⟧ son of Imlah, whom he hates. The chapter ends with a battle, the fulfilment of a prophecy, and brief notes on Jehoshaphat's reign in Judah and on Ahab's son ⟦p:ahaziah_120|Ahaziah⟧, who now takes the throne in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. His story, and ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧'s, continue directly in Second Kings.
